Lecture at a glance

  • Teeth & supporting structures → enamel, dentin, pulp chamber, periodontal ligament
  • Inflammatory lesions → dental caries, gingivitis, periodontitis
  • Fibrous proliferative lesions → irritation fibroma, pyogenic granuloma
  • Inflammatory/reactive ulcerations → aphthous ulcer
  • Infections → herpes simplex (acute herpetic gingivostomatitis, herpes labialis), oral candidiasis
  • Tumors & pre-cancerous lesions → leukoplakia spectrum, erythroplakia, squamous cell carcinoma
  • Odontogenic cysts & tumors → periapical cyst, dentigerous cyst, ameloblastoma

Main framework: the precancer → cancer pathway

Hyperkeratosis
→
Hyperplasia/Acanthosis
→
Epithelial dysplasia
→
Carcinoma-in-Situ
→
Invasive SCCA

Leukoplakia: spectrum of lesions (lecture order). The key step to invasion is a breach in the basement membrane.

A. Teeth and Supporting Structures p. 1

StructureLecture features
Enamel
  • Exposed from the gum
  • Hard, inert, acellular tissue
  • Considered the most mineralized tissue of the body
Dentin
  • Cellular
  • Specialized connective tissue making up most of the hard part of the tooth
Pulp chamber
  • Loose connective tissue stroma
  • Rich in nerve bundles, lymphatics, and capillaries
Periodontal ligament Must Know
  • Attaches the teeth to the alveolar ridge of the jaw
  • Strong flexible attachment to withstand mastication
Must Know The periodontal ligament attaches teeth to the alveolar bone.
Inflammation in this area could lead to eventual teeth loss. (Review Q7)
Do Not Confuse Enamel = acellular, most mineralized.
Dentin = cellular, makes up most of the hard part.

B. Inflammatory Lesions

Dental Caries Must Know p. 1

  • Most common cause of tooth loss before 35 years old.
  • Usually brought about by poor oral hygiene
  • Incidence has decreased due to improved oral hygiene and fluoridation of water
    • Fluoride incorporates into the crystalline structure of enamel thus forming fluorapatite which is resistant to bacterial acid degradation

Pathogenesis

Bacteria within oral cavity ferment food sugars
→
Produce acid metabolic end products
→
Mineral dissolution of the tooth structure

Gingivitis Must Know pp. 1-2

  • Inflammation of soft tissues surrounding the gingiva (teeth and the gum).
    • Can be improved by brushing, flossing, and regular dental visits.
  • Most prevalent and severe in adolescents

Pathogenesis

Lack of proper oral hygiene
↓
Formation of dental plaque
↓
Continuous build-up of plaque
↓
Plaque mineralization
↓
Calculus (Tartar) formation
↓
Continuous build-up of plaque
↓
Plaque build up beneath gum line
↓
Gingivitis (inflammation and reddening)
  • Dental plaque: complex mass consisting of
    • microorganisms from the normal flora
    • saliva proteins
    • desquamated epithelial cells
Case 1 19 y/o male with halitosis and gum bleeding after toothbrushing. Gum swelling, redness and puffiness around the tooth.
Diagnosis: Gingivitis
  • Soft tissue swelling surrounding the teeth and gums
  • Common cause: Plaque-induced and common among adolescents
    • Plaque pushes against the gums, causing inflammation
  • Disease prevention: Brushing softly and slowly, or by using soft bristle toothbrushes

Periodontitis Must Know pp. 2-3

Definition: Inflammation of the periodontal ligaments, alveolar bone, and cementum.

Common causative organisms

  • Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans
  • Porphyromonas gingivalis
  • Prevotella intermedia
  • There are 300 types of oral bacteria. Facultative gram-positive bacteria are found in healthy gums.

Pathogenesis

Marked shift in types and proportion of bacteria along the gingiva
↓
Predominance of anaerobic and microaerophilic gram-negative flora + environmental factors (poor oral hygiene)
↓
Periodontitis
↓ worsening
Complete destruction of periodontal ligament and alveolar bone
↓
Loosening and eventual loss of teeth
Must Know Among the inflammatory lesions of the oral cavity, only periodontitis can serve both as a component and an etiological factor in systemic diseases.
  • Component of systemic diseases: AIDS, leukemia, DM
  • Etiologic factor in systemic diseases: infective endocarditis, pulmonary and brain abscesses
Case 43 y/o male construction worker with easy gum bleeding while brushing. Marked gingival recession with erythema, extensive plaque and tartar, deep pocket spaces between teeth.
Diagnosis: Periodontitis, secondary to the effect of dental plaque formation driven by oral bacterial flora.
Advise regular dental cleaning and gentle tooth brushing to prevent further gingival recession and bleeding.
Exam Trap (Review Q3) Periodontitis = altered composition of the oral microbiome with gram-negative flora, not gram-positive.
"Most common cause of tooth loss before 35" = dental caries, not periodontitis.
"Inflammation of soft tissues surrounding the tooth/gum" = gingivitis.

C. Fibrous Proliferative Lesions p. 3

  • May present as tumor masses or ulcerations

Four types

Irritation Fibroma 61%
Peripheral ossifying fibroma 22%
Pyogenic granuloma 12%
Peripheral giant-cell granuloma 5%

Irritation Fibroma Must Know p. 3

  • Known as traumatic fibroma or focal fibrous hyperplasia.
  • This usually occurs after a history of trauma.
  • Commonly observed within the buccal mucosa (biteline) and gingivodental margin.
  • Reactive proliferation of fibrous tissue from repetitive trauma

Gross:

  • Exophytic nodule or bump with a smooth surface
  • Has the same color as the surrounding mucosa

Histopathology:

  • Proliferation of fibrous tissue infiltrated by few inflammatory cells and covered by squamous mucosa
Case 45 y/o female teacher. 0.6 cm pink mucosa-covered mass next to the first molar on the lower right, on the bite line. Excision was done with no recurrence.
Diagnosis: Irritation fibroma → common neoplasm resulting from reactive hyperplasia of the fibrous connective tissue in response to irritation or trauma.

Pyogenic Granuloma Must Know pp. 3-4

Clinical: Gingiva of children, young adults, and pregnant women.

  • Capacity to regress or undergo fibrous maturation and develop into a peripheral ossifying fibroma and recur.

Gross:

  • Circumscribed, elevated, sessile/pedunculated, soft, red to purple mass
  • May be ulcerated due to its size, which may reach up to 2-5 cm

Histopathology:

  • Lobular proliferation of small blood vessels
  • Edematous stroma with acute and chronic inflammation
  • Highly vascular pedunculated lesion composed of organized granulation tissue with mixed inflammatory cells
  • Proliferation of various-sized blood vessels, and dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates
Case 2 35 y/o G2P2 female with a 2 cm soft red mass in the left lower gum line.
Diagnosis: Pyogenic granuloma
  • Highly vascular lesion (Picture D shows RBCs)
  • Organized granulation tissue
  • Mixed inflammatory cells (Picture B: small-sized blood vessels with inflammatory cells, either lymphoplasmacytic or neutrophilic)
  • A granulation tissue covered by thickened squamous epithelium signifies pyogenic granuloma
  • Can regress on its own
  • If chronic irritant persists → can develop into a peripheral ossifying fibroma
  • Overall, a pyogenic granuloma is a benign lesion
Exam Trap (Review Q4) Pyogenic granuloma DOES NOT mature into a peripheral giant cell granuloma.
It matures into a peripheral ossifying fibroma.
Key Differentiator Irritation fibroma = fibrous tissue, few inflammatory cells, same color as mucosa, bite line.
Pyogenic granuloma = highly vascular granulation tissue, red to purple, gingiva, pregnant women.

D. Inflammatory/Reactive Ulcerations p. 4

Two types: Traumatic ulcers and Aphthous ulcers

Aphthous Ulcer (Canker Sores) Must Know pp. 4-5

Clinical: Painful, recurrent ulcers

Cause: Unknown (idiopathic)

Gross:

  • Single/multiple, shallow, hyperemic ulcers
  • Covered by a thin exudate

Histopathology:

  • Initially mononuclear inflammatory cells
  • Acute inflammatory cells may be present if there is a secondary bacterial infection
  • If biopsy is done (not recommended) → initial predominance of lymphoplasmacytic cells with some neutrophils if secondary bacterial infection
Case 17 y/o female student, 2 days before the end of finals. Painful, small, gray-white lesion on the lower lip. Afebrile, no alcohol or tobacco use. 0.3 cm shallow ulcer with an erythematous rim. Disappeared after 10 days.
Should you prescribe medication? No. This is an aphthous ulcer ("singaw").
  • Usually appears during periods of stress and is never large
  • Usually observed in the first two decades of life
  • May last 7-10 days or persist for weeks
Exam Trap (Review Q1) Lesion that will probably NOT have a history of trauma → Aphthous ulcer (unknown etiology).
Irritation fibroma and periapical cyst can follow trauma.

Herpes Simplex Infection Must Know p. 5

Also known as: Cold sores or Fever Blisters

Cause:

  • HSV-1 (Oral Herpes)
  • HSV-2 (Genital Herpes, few oral infections)

Presentation:

  • Abrupt onset of vesicles and ulcers in the oral cavity (lip or gingiva)
  • Fever, anorexia, lymphadenopathy, and irritability
  • Primary herpetic infection: acute herpetic gingivostomatitis

Acute Herpetic Gingivostomatitis

Histologic findings:

  • Acantholysis: Loss of desmosomes → cell separation
    • Manifests as intracellular and intercellular edema
  • Intranuclear viral inclusion (Cowdry Type A inclusion bodies)
  • Multinucleated giant cells (polykaryons) in Tzanck smears
  • Vesicles of herpes simplex usually clear within 2-4 weeks
    • Virus can still be present in the regional nerves and become dormant in the local ganglia

Herpes Labialis

  • Due to HSV reactivation
  • Common vesicular lesion (cold sores or fever blisters)
  • Appears in young adults
  • Recurrent or triggered by: URTI, stress, wind, sunlight, cold weather, menstruation

Oral Candidiasis (Thrush) Must Know pp. 5, 7-8

Etiology:

  • Overgrowth of Candida albicans (normal oral flora)
  • Most common fungal infection of the oral cavity
  • Indicator of poor immune status of patient

Clinical forms:

  • Pseudomembranous
    • Most common
    • Includes thrush
    • Formation of superficial gray-white inflammatory membrane of matted organisms within a fibrinous suppurative exudate
  • Erythematous
  • Hyperplastic
Case 28 y/o HIV patient. CC: thick white membrane covering the tongue and palate.
Diagnosis: Oral candidiasis (oral thrush)
  • Superficial gray to white membrane
  • Opportunistic infection because the patient has HIV
  • Oral thrush alone sometimes signals a poor immune response. If there are no other comorbidities (i.e. chronic steroid use), they sometimes have HIV
  • Histologically: pseudohyphal elements

F. Tumors and Pre-cancerous Lesions of the Oral Cavity pp. 5-6

Brought about by history of chronic irritation, chronic smoking, and alcohol abuse

Leukoplakia Must Know pp. 5-6, 8

Definition (WHO): Clinical term used to describe a white patch or plaque that cannot be scraped off

  • Cannot be characterized clinically or pathologically as any other disease
    • If you have ruled out every other disease and it is only a white patch or plaque anywhere in the oral cavity, it is leukoplakia
  • A premalignant lesion (5-25%)

Common locations:

Buccal mucosa
Floor of the mouth
Ventral surface of the tongue
Palate
Gingiva
Must Know · Lecturer 📣 Differentiated from oral thrush, which can be scraped off since it is a mass of matted organisms.
If oral thrush is scraped off, a red, inflamed tongue or mucosa is usually revealed underneath, whereas leukoplakia remains white.
If you…Diagnosis
Are able to scrape it off, and see fungal elements under the microscopeOral thrush
Are unable to scrape it offLeukoplakia

Leukoplakia: Spectrum of Lesions Must Know p. 6

Hyperkeratosis
→
Hyperplasia/Acanthosis
→
Epithelial dysplasia
→
Carcinoma-in-Situ
→
Invasive SCCA

Hyperkeratosis p. 6

  • Thickening of superficial layer of the squamous epithelium
  • (+/-) Epithelial dysplasia (may/may not be present)

Hyperplasia/Acanthosis pp. 6, 8

  • Thickening of the squamous mucosa
  • Also known as acanthosis. Elongated and thickened Rete ridges
    • Increased number of squamous cells present in the area
Exam Trap (Review Q8) Histologic term referring to epidermal hyperplasia → Acanthosis.
Hyperkeratosis = thickening of the superficial (keratin) layer, not hyperplasia.

Epithelial Dysplasia Must Know pp. 6, 8

Mild/Moderate Epithelial DysplasiaSevere Epithelial Dysplasia
GradeLow grade squamous intraepithelial lesionHigh grade squamous intraepithelial lesion
Disordered maturationInner ⅓ of the mucosaInner ⅔ to ¾ of the mucosa
Involved squamous cells
  • Hyperchromasia (darkened nuclei)
  • Active mitosis
  • Enlarged nuclei
  • More hyperchromasia and atypical
  • Lots of mitotic figures
  • Enlarged nuclei
Basement membrane—Dysplastic cells do not go beyond the basement membrane (no breach)

Erythroplakia Must Know p. 6

AKA: Dysplastic leukoplakia

Gross:

  • Red, velvety patches
  • Eroded areas usually remain level with or slightly depressed from the surrounding mucosa
  • Higher risk of malignant transformation (50%)

Histology:

  • Carcinoma-in-situ or severe dysplasia
  • Increased inflammation with vascular dilation

Demographics: Usually seen in males (2:1) around ages 40-70

Clinical Cue (Review Q2) Red gingival lesion + biopsy with full-thickness dysplasia and severe vascular dilation → Erythroplakia.
Key Differentiator (Review Q5) Leukoplakia = white, premalignant 5-25%.
Erythroplakia = red, velvety, 50%.
Leukoplakia has a lower risk of malignant transformation than erythroplakia.

Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCCA) pp. 7-8

General Must Know

  • Represents 95% of head and neck cancers
    • Remaining 5%: Adenocarcinoma of the salivary gland
  • Aggressive epithelial malignancy
  • 6th most common neoplasm in the world
  • Most of the malignancies in the oral cavity are squamous cell carcinomas

Etiopathogenesis

Most commonOthers
Tobacco
Pipe smoking
Alcohol		HPV-16
Genetic
Actinic radiation: CA of lower lip
Betel nut chewing
Chronic mucosal irritation

Location

Lip 45% (most common site)
Tongue 16%
Floor of mouth 12%
Gingiva 12%
Buccal mucosa 10%
Hard palate 5%

Spread

  • Can metastasize in the cervical lymph nodes
    • Can also metastasize to distant sites: mediastinal lymph nodes, lungs, liver, and bone
  • Appearance of SCCA on one site would be the same on other sites, depending on differentiation

Histology Must Know

  • Resembles the upper skin tissue
  • Nests of atypical squamous cells with large round/ovoid hyperchromatic nuclei
  • Abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm
  • May have keratinization (glassy-pink appearance)
  • Intercellular bridging seen on high-power objective ("highway sa gitna ng cells")
  • Tumor nest usually spreads from the overlying squamous epithelium into the stroma
Must Know: Differentiation Differentiation is based on the pleomorphism of the cells and presence of keratin pearls.
Abundant keratin pearls or squamous eddies → well-differentiated SCCA.
The more keratin pearls present, the more likely it is well-differentiated.
Intercellular bridges are also abundant and distinct.
Key Differentiator Severe epithelial dysplasia (severe leukoplakia) → atypical cells in ⅔ to ¾ of the epithelium, mitotic figures, lack of maturation, but no breach in the basement membrane.
SCC → there is already a breach in the basement membrane.

G. Odontogenic Cysts and Tumors pp. 8-10

  • Odontogenic cysts originate from the remnants of dentine (odontogenic) epithelium
  • Classified as developmental or inflammatory

Histologic Classification of Odontogenic Cysts

InflammatoryDevelopmental
Periapical cyst
Residual cyst
Paradental cyst		Dentigerous cyst
Odontogenic keratocyst
Gingival cyst of newborn
Gingival cyst of adult
Eruption cyst
Lateral periodontal cyst
Glandular odontogenic cyst
Calcifying epithelial odontogenic cyst (Gorlin cyst)

Periapical Cyst Must Know pp. 8-10

AKA: Radicular Cyst

  • 10% of inflammatory cysts of oral mucosa
  • Due to inflammation of dental pulp from caries or trauma

X-ray: Round or flask-shaped radiolucency with radiopaque margin

Histology:

  • Arcaded pattern of epithelial lining (due to arc appearance), usually with numerous chronic inflammatory cells

Treatment:

  • Excision alone is the treatment (for benign cysts)
  • If the area is not thoroughly cleaned → prone to recurrence
Case 17 y/o male soccer player hit in the face with a soccer ball. CC: cyst on periapical area of front tooth.
Diagnosis: Periapical/Radicular cyst → inflammation of the pulp (dental caries, trauma). Radiolucent flask-shaped cyst. Arcaded epithelium with numerous chronic inflammatory cells.

Dentigerous Cyst Must Know p. 9

  • Most common odontogenic cyst
  • Unilocular lesions usually present as a missing tooth
  • Result of fluid accumulation between the developing tooth and the dental follicle
  • Involves permanent impacted molars (wisdom tooth)
    • Originates around the crown of an unerupted permanent tooth (answer key)

Histology: Thin layer of stratified squamous epithelium with dense chronic inflammation

Clinical Cue (Review Q10) Cystic mass near the 3rd molar + X-ray unilocular radiolucency surrounding an unerupted tooth → Dentigerous cyst.

Ameloblastoma Must Know pp. 9-10

AKA: Adamantinoma

  • Benign odontogenic tumor derived from odontogenic epithelium or ectomesenchyme
  • Derived from the ameloblasts or dental lamina
  • Commonly cystic, slow-growing and locally invasive
  • Tissue growth is very aggressive in the involved area
    • Has indolent course but is grossly disfiguring
  • May be solid, multicystic or unicystic

Location:

80%: Posterior mandible (70% arising from the molar-ramus area)
20%: Posterior maxillary

X-ray: Multilocular radiolucency with well-defined corticated and scalloped margin → Honey-comb or soap-bubble appearance

Histology:

  • Discrete varisized islands of odontogenic epithelium in fibrous connective tissue stroma
  • Peripheral layer of columnar or cuboidal cells
  • Islands of epithelium resembling the enamel organ may be appreciated
  • Peripheral ameloblastic columnar epithelium surrounding areas of stellate reticulum-like cells
Must Know: Clinical Behavior High recurrence rate (up to 90%) if there is inadequate resection.
It is important to excise with adequate bone margins.
Clinical Cue (Review Q6 and Q9) Tall columnar palisading epithelium with central areas of stellate cells → Ameloblastoma.
TRUE of ameloblastoma: most cases arise in the posterior mandible. It is slow-growing, not rapidly growing.
Do Not Confuse: X-ray Periapical cyst → round or flask-shaped radiolucency with radiopaque margin, at the tooth apex.
Dentigerous cyst → unilocular, around the crown of an unerupted/impacted tooth.
Ameloblastoma → multilocular, honey-comb or soap-bubble.

Cram Sheet

Core Definitions

  • Periodontal ligament → attaches teeth to alveolar ridge. Inflammation → teeth loss
  • Enamel → hard, inert, acellular, most mineralized tissue
  • Gingivitis → inflammation of soft tissues surrounding the gingiva
  • Periodontitis → inflammation of PDL, alveolar bone, and cementum
  • Leukoplakia → white patch or plaque that cannot be scraped off and cannot be characterized as any other disease
  • Erythroplakia → AKA dysplastic leukoplakia, red velvety patches
  • Acanthosis → hyperplasia (elongated, thickened Rete ridges)
  • Hyperkeratosis → thickening of superficial layer
  • Acantholysis → loss of desmosomes → cell separation (HSV)

Caries: bacteria ferment sugars
→

→

Gingivitis: poor hygiene
→
plaque
→
mineralization → calculus
→
plaque beneath gum line
→
gingivitis
Periodontitis: shift to gram-negative anaerobes
→
PDL + alveolar bone destruction
→
tooth loss

→
fluorapatite
→
resistant to bacterial acid

Classic Associations

  • Periodontitis organisms
    • Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans, Porphyromonas gingivalis, Prevotella intermedia
    • Component of: AIDS, leukemia, DM
    • Etiologic factor for: infective endocarditis, pulmonary and brain abscesses
  • SCCA risk
    • Most common: tobacco, pipe smoking, alcohol
    • Also: HPV-16, genetic, betel nut, chronic irritation
    • Actinic radiation → CA of lower lip
  • Herpes labialis triggers → URTI, stress, wind, sunlight, cold weather, menstruation
  • Candidiasis forms → pseudomembranous (most common, thrush), erythematous, hyperplastic

Diagnostic Anchors (Histology)

FindingThink
Fibrous tissue, few inflammatory cells, squamous mucosaIrritation fibroma
Lobular small vessels, organized granulation tissuePyogenic granuloma
Acantholysis, Cowdry Type A, polykaryons (Tzanck)Herpes simplex
Pseudohyphal elementsCandidiasis
Keratin pearls, intercellular bridges, BM breachedSCCA (more pearls = well-differentiated)
Arcaded epithelium + chronic inflammatory cellsPeriapical cyst
Thin stratified squamous epithelium + dense chronic inflammationDentigerous cyst
Peripheral palisading columnar cells + stellate reticulum-like cellsAmeloblastoma

If You See X → Think Y

  • Tooth loss before 35 → dental caries
  • Adolescent, bleeding puffy gums → gingivitis
  • Recession, tartar, deep pockets → periodontitis
  • Mucosa-colored nodule on bite line → irritation fibroma
  • Pregnant woman, red gingival mass → pyogenic granuloma
  • Stress, small painful ulcer with erythematous rim → aphthous ulcer (no meds)
  • White membrane that scrapes off, HIV → oral candidiasis
  • White patch that cannot be scraped off → leukoplakia
  • Red velvety lesion, full-thickness dysplasia, vascular dilation → erythroplakia
  • Trauma/caries, flask-shaped lucency at apex → periapical cyst
  • Unilocular lucency around unerupted 3rd molar → dentigerous cyst
  • Posterior mandible, soap-bubble multilocular → ameloblastoma

Common Confusions & Exam Traps

  • Pyogenic granuloma → peripheral ossifying fibroma, NOT peripheral giant cell granuloma
  • Periodontitis flora = gram-negative. Healthy gums = facultative gram-positive
  • Leukoplakia has a lower malignant risk than erythroplakia
  • Severe dysplasia = no breach of basement membrane. SCC = breach
  • Epidermal hyperplasia = acanthosis, not hyperkeratosis
  • Aphthous ulcer = no trauma history (idiopathic)
  • Ameloblastoma is slow-growing and locally invasive, benign, but grossly disfiguring

Warnings / Management

  • Aphthous ulcer → do not prescribe medication. Biopsy not recommended
  • Periapical cyst → excision alone. Not thoroughly cleaned → recurrence
  • Ameloblastoma → excise with adequate bone margins, else up to 90% recurrence
  • Periodontitis → regular dental cleaning and gentle tooth brushing
